content: Caesarean section is the most frequently performed major surgical procedure on women globally. The techniques used during this operation, including the type of abdominal incision, vary, and some of these methods have been evaluated through randomized controlled trials. The objective of this review was to assess the benefits and risks associated with different types of abdominal surgical incisions used during caesarean sections. The data for this review were obtained from the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register as of February 28, 2013. Only randomized controlled trials that compared different abdominal incisions for caesarean sections were included. Data were extracted, verified for accuracy, and analyzed. Four studies involving a total of 666 women were included in this review. Two of these studies, which included 411 women, compared the Joel-Cohen incision with the Pfannenstiel incision. The results showed that the Joel-Cohen incision was associated with a 65% reduction in postoperative febrile morbidity (risk ratio [RR] 0.35, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.14 to 0.87). Additionally, one of these trials reported several other benefits of the Joel-Cohen incision compared to the Pfannenstiel incision. These included reduced postoperative analgesic requirements (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.76), shorter operating time (mean difference [MD] -11.40 minutes, 95% CI -16.55 to -6.25), shorter delivery time (MD -1.90 minutes, 95% CI -2.53 to -1.27), lower total dose of analgesia required in the first 24 hours (MD -0.89, 95% CI -1.19 to -0.59), reduced estimated blood loss (MD -58.00 mL, 95% CI -108.51 to -7.49), shorter postoperative hospital stay for the mother (MD -1.50 days, 95% CI -2.16 to -0.84), and a longer time to the first dose of analgesia (MD 0.80 hours, 95% CI 0.12 to 1.48). No other significant differences were observed between the two groups in these trials. Two additional studies compared muscle-cutting incisions with the Pfannenstiel incision. One of these studies, which involved 68 women and compared the Mouchel incision with the Pfannenstiel incision, did not contribute data to this review. The other study, which included 97 women and compared the Maylard muscle-cutting incision with the Pfannenstiel incision, found no significant differences in febrile morbidity (RR 1.26, 95% CI 0.08 to 19.50), the need for blood transfusion (RR 0.42, 95% CI 0.02 to 9.98), wound infection rates (RR 1.26, 95% CI 0.27 to 5.91), physical muscle strength tests at three months postoperatively, or postoperative hospital stay (MD 0.40 days, 95% CI -0.34 to 1.14). In conclusion, the Joel-Cohen incision offers several advantages over the Pfannenstiel incision, including reduced postoperative fever, pain, and analgesic requirements, as well as less blood loss, shorter surgery duration, and shorter hospital stays. These benefits for the mother may also translate into cost savings for the healthcare system. However, the trials included in this review did not provide data on severe or long-term morbidity and mortality outcomes.
